$comment: Shared conformance cases for Kerna's two enforcement points: permissions.rs (Rust,
in-loop) and enforce.py (Python, model seam). Semantics are specified in POLICY.md.
Duplicated in the kerna repository at benchmarks/policy/policy-conformance.json
because the two halves are separate artifacts today. Each engine's test prints the
SHA-256 of its copy; when you edit one, edit both.
Every case states its default explicitly. P5 keeps the install defaults different by
enforcement point, so a suite that relied on a default would test the wrong thing.
`expect` uses the shared vocabulary: allow | deny | require_confirmation.
At the model seam require_confirmation resolves to deny (P4); the seam test asserts
that mapping rather than the raw level.

cases.name: an allowlist works regardless of rule order
cases.why: The idiom nearly every real policy takes. This is the case that was broken: the seam matched first-rule-wins and denied Read.

cases.name: an allowlist works when the exact rule comes first too
cases.why: Order must not matter across specificity levels, in either direction.

cases.name: a denylist over a permissive wildcard
the first of two rules naming the same tool wins
cases.why: Order still decides within one specificity level, which is what makes a narrow predicate before a broad fallback useful.

cases.name: the first of two wildcards wins
an unlisted tool takes the stated default
cases.why: Stated per case, never inherited, because the install defaults differ by enforcement point on purpose.

cases.name: an unlisted tool under a permissive default
an empty policy is entirely its default
require_confirmation is carried as its own level
cases.why: In-loop it prompts. At the seam there is no human to ask, so it denies -- the seam test asserts the mapping.

cases.name: an exact require_confirmation beats a permissive wildcard
tool names are matched exactly, not by prefix
cases.why: A prefix match would let `Read` silently govern `ReadSecrets`.

cases.name: matching is case sensitive
cases.why: Tool names are identifiers. Case-insensitive matching would make `bash` a way around a rule on `Bash`.
